extracted.intended_audience: aspiring fiction writers / students of creative writing
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for revising short stories and novels, covering macro- and micro-revision: description, dialogue, pacing, setting, voice, theme, sentence-level craft, and preparing a finished, publishable manuscript.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concrete description / particular over general
rubrics_metrics.description: With description, the particular always trumps the general, and concrete always trumps abstract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor specific, striking details (e.g., 'hair streamed like turnings of steaming copper and bronze') rather than bland generalities ('beautiful strawberry-blond hair'). Use modifiers that provide concrete sensory jolts; avoid abstract adjectives when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selective use of concrete details (the 'quick' vs the 'dead')
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose details selectively: D. H. Lawrence's distinction between 'the quick' (lifeblood) and 'the dead'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lead with the 'quick' things—the first things readers notice—rather than filling scenes with irrelevant, 'dead' details. Be economical and intentional about which particulars you show.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dialogue — concision
rubrics_metrics.description: Concise: the fewer words to make a point, the better.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trim dialogue to the minimal words that achieve the purpose; avoid tape-recorder realism and overly long, aimless speech. Read dialogue aloud to ensure speakability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dialogue — subtext
rubrics_metrics.description: Subtext: it's not what characters say, but what they mean, that counts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write dialogue that implies underlying motives and emotions rather than stating them outright; use implication and tension to reveal character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dialogue — illogical and adversarial realism
rubrics_metrics.description: Illogical: people are illogical, especially when they speak. Adversarial: they should argue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow characters to be illogical and to disagree. Conflict in dialogue reveals character and advances plot. Avoid making characters perfectly rational or harmoniously agreeable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dialogue — speakable and avoid forced voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Dialogue should be speakable and not forced into characters' mouths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If characters are well-motivated, their speech should arise naturally; the writer acts as a stenographer. Read dialogue aloud; avoid inventing unnatural 'voice' that calls attention to itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of scene and summary / pacing
rubrics_metrics.description: Pay attention to the ratio of scene to summary, of dialogue to description. This relates to pacing and decisions about compressing or expanding events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Layer scene with summary; emulate roller-coaster pacing (slow climbs, swift falls) when appropriate. Recognize that fast-paced is quantitative not qualitative—different authors favor different balances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Setting — ground reader in time and place
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers should be grounded in the time and place of stories; context is everything.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use explicit cues (dates, posters) or subtle markers (smog, wrought iron) to establish setting. Setting functions as character and shapes plot and atmosphere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Setting — use setting metaphorically
rubrics_metrics.description: Look for ways to use setting metaphorically to amplify theme or mood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ landscapes and environmental details as symbolic or thematic devices (e.g., Bleak House's fog evoking the murkiness of the court system).

rubrics_metrics.name: Flashbacks — keep them brief and scene-aware
rubrics_metrics.description: A flashback is a digression that works; keep flashbacks very brief and aware of the scene's tension limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Know how far a reader's attention can be diverted. Limit flashbacks (often to a paragraph); avoid breaking into full-blown dialogue in a flashback; if a flashback expands into a full scene, relocate it or give it its own section/chapter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voice — make and keep a contract with the reader; consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: With the first paragraphs you make a contract to tell a particular kind of story in a particular voice; do it consistently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop consistent tics/mannerisms into a coherent narrator's voice. Do something weird consistently and it becomes style; stray weirdness looks like mistakes. Take a stand with material and hold the chosen voice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid journalese; cultivate musical prose
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalese delivers necessary information but lacks music and voice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for language that rewards re-reading—music, figurative devices, sentence rhythms—rather than merely functional prose that is read once.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voice — take risks appropriate to character
rubrics_metrics.description: Writing powerfully means taking risks (e.g., using a strong first-person utterance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match voice intensity to character: strong characters may warrant forceful, commanding sentences; weak characters can be rendered with a voice of weakness—but be decisive and consistent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theme — discover through writing and then nurture
rubrics_metrics.description: Writers often 'write to discover' themes; themes emerge from the material and must then be recognized and highlighted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When themes appear, make them resonate (recurring images, motifs), dress them up subtly and display them repeatedly without heavy-handedness (e.g., Gatsby's green light).

rubrics_metrics.name: Focused revision — work on one craft element at a time
rubrics_metrics.description: When revising, force yourself to focus solely on a single craft element (POV, dialogue, setting, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do successive rounds of revision each addressing a different major craft element to avoid being overwhelmed by juggling many changes at once.

rubrics_metrics.name: Microrevision — sweat the small stuff; read aloud
rubrics_metrics.description: After addressing big-picture issues, engage in microrevision: read aloud and mark anything that trips you up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Line-edit for stylistic precision; use trusted colleagues for feedback while remaining the final judge of changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grammar and punctuation — know conventions before breaking them
rubrics_metrics.description: Grammar is a convention writers may depart from, but only with good reason and after mastering it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learn usage rules (recommendation: The Elements of Style). Use grammar to remain clear; breaking conventions ignorantly can make you appear careless or 'dumb.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overuse of imperfect 'to be' verbs
rubrics_metrics.description: The imperfect tense ('was', 'were', etc.) is 'dead' when overused and paints no picture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer active, evocative verbs (e.g., 'he wore' vs 'he was wearing'; 'she ran' vs 'she was running') to give prose energy and specificity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metaphors — prefer metaphors, avoid mixed metaphors
rubrics_metrics.description: If you can change a simile into a metaphor without confusing readers, do so. Don't mix metaphors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep metaphorical imagery consistent (unchanged register and domain). Avoid mishmashes that confuse the sensory field or register.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modifiers — use adjectives and adverbs boldly but sparingly
rubrics_metrics.description: Modifiers are often 'dead wood'; use them only when they add something new.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose stronger nouns and verbs so you need fewer modifiers. When modifiers are used, let them surprise or deepen understanding (e.g., Joseph Heller's inventive modifiers). Use them like spices—sparingly and boldly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kill clichés
rubrics_metrics.description: Clichés are tired figures of speech that insult the reader; recognize familiar groupings of words as clichés.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replace clichéd phrases (e.g., 'It's raining cats and dogs', 'a heart of stone') with fresh language. Even gorgeous lines risk cliché if overused; strive for originality in expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attributions — prefer 'said' and keep tags invisible
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid 'said'-avoidance theatrics; 'said' is smooth and discreet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't over-ornament dialogue tags with 'chuckled', 'barked', 'opined', etc., unless purposeful. Other attribution schemes can work (authors avoiding 'said' entirely), but the tag should not call attention away from the dialogue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid Latinisms and pretentious words
rubrics_metrics.description: Latinisms are unnecessarily bulky words (ascertain, perpetrate) when plain words will do.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer simple verbs (talk vs converse; buy vs purchase). Be on the lookout for '-tion', '-ism', '-ness', '-ment' words and prune pretentiousness. Simplify where possible; readers will thank you.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cutting — omit needless words; be merciless
rubrics_metrics.description: Writers must cut mercilessly; 'omit needless words.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be willing to cut entire passages; a text that can work in fewer words should. Let the reader participate—imply rather than overexplain. Try cutting by a third as an exercise and evaluate improvement after a break.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tweaking — craft sentences and re-orchestrate prose
rubrics_metrics.description: Tweaking is reworking sentences and paragraphs to be as clear, pungent, and crisp as possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shift words, change rhythms, and test alternatives. Tweaking requires experience; practice, accept that many attempts will be worse, and learn from them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowing when a piece is done
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize the law of diminishing returns and that some writers 'abandon' rather than finish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Declare victory when further revisions yield negligible improvement or when form and meaning align and words feel inevitable. Publication or external constraints can also determine 'done-ness.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Manuscript as product — finish the complete work
rubrics_metrics.description: To get published you must produce a completed piece (not just an idea or a few pages).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Finished first draft is essential; editors and agents expect a complete manuscript. Partials and pitches rarely substitute for the completed work unless you already have a substantial sales record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make the product appealing — quality control
rubrics_metrics.description: Make agents and publishers want your product by ensuring it is outstandingly good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors and agents are busy—don't expect them to discover hidden merit. Consider using a manuscript analyst or other professional feedback to raise quality. Treat writing as a product to be made attractive to its market.
